procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of District & Sessions Judge dated 31.07.2008
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondent appealed to the High Court against the order of the District & Sessions Judge dated 31.07.2008. The High Court allowed the appeal and quashed the order of the District Judge dated 31.07.2008 as well as the complaint filed pursuant thereto.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Aggrieved by the High Court's judgment, the appellant filed an appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 359 of 2018) before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant's case falls under Section 195(1)(b)(i) of the Cr.P.C., making the Constitution Bench judgment in Iqbal Singh Marwah inapplicable, despite the appellant having consistently argued the case under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) before the lower courts.

facts: The appellant argued before the Supreme Court that their case should be considered under Section 195(1)(b)(i) of the Cr.P.C.
This was a change in argument, as the appellant had consistently framed their case under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) in the lower courts (Session Court and High Court).
The appellant's original application (No. 95 of 2007) and the initial favorable order from the District Judge both specifically referred to Section 195(1)(b)(ii).
The appellant changed their argument to try and avoid the applicability of the Constitution Bench judgment in *Iqbal Singh Marwah*, which interpreted Section 195(1)(b)(ii).
law: A party cannot change its fundamental legal argument at a later stage of litigation after having consistently pursued a different one in the lower courts.

The Constitution Bench in *Iqbal Singh Marwah* held that when an offense involving a document is committed *before* that document is produced or given in evidence in court, the procedural bar under Section 195 (including subsections (b)(i) and (b)(ii)) does not apply.
application: The Court refused to allow the appellant to "turn round" and change their argument from Section 195(1)(b)(ii) to Section 195(1)(b)(i) at the Supreme Court stage.
The Court noted that the appellant's own complaint and the favorable order they initially received from the District Judge were explicitly based on Section 195(1)(b)(ii).

The Court further reasoned that even if the argument was considered, the principle from *Iqbal Singh Marwah* would still be relevant, as it clarified that the bar under Section 195 does not apply to offenses committed before a document is brought into court proceedings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the appellant was bound by their consistent position in the lower courts that the case fell under Section 195(1)(b)(ii). Since the appellant had specifically invoked that section throughout the proceedings, it was not open for them to change their stance to avoid the binding precedent of *Iqbal Singh Marwah*. The Court, therefore, upheld the High Court's decision.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant's case falls under Section 195(1)(b)(i) of the Cr.P.C., making the Constitution Bench judgment in Iqbal Singh Marwah inapplicable, despite the appellant having consistently argued the case under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) before the lower courts.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred in applying the Constitution Bench judgment in Iqbal Singh Marwah, as that judgment pertains to Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Cr.P.C.
The allegations made in the appellant's complaint are actually referable to Section 195(1)(b)(i) of the Cr.P.C., making the Iqbal Singh Marwah judgment inapplicable to the facts of the present case.
respondent_arguments: No one appeared on behalf of the respondent to present arguments in this appeal.

cases.case_name: Iqbal Singh Marwah & Anr. v. Meenakshi Marwah & Anr.
cases.principle: The bar contained in Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code is not applicable to a case where the forgery of a document was committed before the document was produced in a court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The bar against the initiation of prosecution proceedings under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) does not apply when the act of forgery was perpetrated prior to the document's production in court.
obiter: If the language of a legislation is capable of more than one interpretation, the one which is capable of causing mischievous consequences should be averted.
If a forger could preempt prosecution by simply producing a forged document in any long-drawn litigation, it would lead to unsavoury consequences.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court rejected the appellant's attempt to re-characterize the case as falling under Section 195(1)(b)(i) of the Cr.P.C. because the appellant had explicitly and consistently framed the case under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) in the lower courts. Consequently, the High Court was correct in applying the Constitution Bench judgment in Iqbal Singh Marwah, which interprets Section 195(1)(b)(ii), and concluding that a complaint could not be proceeded with under that specific provision.
legal_tests_applied: The rule from Iqbal Singh Marwah & Anr. v. Meenakshi Marwah & Anr. that "Section 195(1)(b)(ii) CrPC would be attracted only when the offences enumerated in the said provision have been committed with respect to a document after it has been produced or given in evidence in a proceeding in any court i.e. during the time when the document was in custodia legis."
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's own application in the lower court explicitly prayed for an inquiry and a written complaint to be made "as per the provision contemplated under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of Criminal Procedure Code."

The appellant could not change the entire legal basis of his case from Section 195(1)(b)(ii) to Section 195(1)(b)(i) for the first time before the Supreme Court merely to circumvent the binding precedent of Iqbal Singh Marwah.
The Court fully endorsed the High Court's view that the present case was not one where a complaint could have been proceeded with under Section 195(1)(b)(ii), thereby finding no merit in the appeal.
why_respondent_won: The High Court correctly applied the binding precedent of Iqbal Singh Marwah to the case as it was framed by the appellant under Section 195(1)(b)(ii).

The application of Iqbal Singh Marwah led to the conclusion that the specific procedure invoked by the appellant—asking the court to file a complaint under Section 195(1)(b)(ii)—was incorrect, resulting in the quashing of the complaint.
The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's judgment, which was in the respondent's favor.
policy_considerations: The Court cited the reasoning from Iqbal Singh Marwah, which seeks to avoid "unsavoury consequences" where a forger could preempt prosecution by simply producing a forged document in a long-drawn litigation, thereby barring a private complaint for the entire pendency of that litigation.

The Court endorsed the principle that if a legislative provision is capable of more than one interpretation, the court should discard the one that leads to an unreasonable result and adopt the interpretation that leads to a "reasonably practicable result".
